issue.issue_text: Whether the insured vehicle was involved in the accident;

facts: Multiple witnesses testified that the vehicle described in the complaint was the one involved in the accident.
The official police investigation report (Final Report under Section 173 of the CrPC) also concluded that the vehicle claimed by the complainants was the one involved.

The Insurance Company presented a witness who suggested a different vehicle with a similar registration number might have been involved, but this witness admitted he was not sure which vehicle was actually in the accident.
law: The burden of proof is on the Insurance Company to establish its defense and prove that the insured vehicle was not involved.
To avoid liability, an insurance company must not only raise a defense but also prove it.
application: The Court weighed the evidence and found that the testimony from various witnesses and the official police report strongly supported the claim that the insured vehicle was involved.

The Court noted that the Insurance Company failed to meet its burden of proof. It did not disprove the claimants' evidence by, for example, calling the investigating officer as a witness or using cross-examination to establish a contrary set of facts.
The Court dismissed the testimony of the Insurance Company's witness as inconclusive, as the witness could not definitively state which vehicle was involved.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Insurance Company failed to prove its claim. Based on the strength of the witness testimonies and the police report, the Court accepted that the insured vehicle was involved in the accident.

issue.issue_text: whether the insurance policy granted by the insurance company covers the incident;

facts: The accident occurred on 11.04.2017 at 14:15 hrs.
The insurance policy was formally issued later on the same day at 15:54 hrs.
The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) found as a matter of fact that the premium for the policy had been paid *before* the accident occurred.
The 'Certificate of Insurance cum Policy Schedule' explicitly stated that the 'Date of commencement of risk' was '11/04/2017' and the 'PERIOD OF INSURANCE' was 'From: 11/04/2017'.
The Insurance Company alleged the policy was obtained by fraud but failed to provide sufficient proof to discharge its onus.
law: The court reiterated the general principle that an insurance policy's effectiveness starts from the time and date specifically incorporated in the policy.
The onus is on the insurance company to prove any allegation of fraud.
application: The Court examined the express terms of the 'Certificate of Insurance cum Policy Schedule'.
It found that the document clearly stated the risk commenced on '11/04/2017', without specifying a particular time. This meant the policy was effective for the entire day of the accident.
The Court also gave weight to the lower court's finding that the premium was paid before the accident, and the delay in issuing the policy was merely due to internal procedures.
Because the policy's own terms were clear, the Court found it unnecessary to delve deeper into case law regarding the exact time of commencement.
The Court also concluded that the Insurance Company could not escape liability by alleging fraud, as it had failed to prove it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the insurance policy covered the incident. It reasoned that the policy's own terms stated that the risk commenced on the date of the accident (11/04/2017), and the insurance company had failed to prove its allegation that the policy was obtained fraudulently.

issue.issue_text: whether the insurance policy was fraudulently obtained.

facts: The Insurance Company's primary argument was that the insurance policy was fraudulently obtained.
The accident occurred at 14:15 hrs, while the insurance policy was formally issued later the same day at 15:54 hrs.
The lower court (MACT) found as a matter of fact that the premium for the policy had been paid *prior* to the accident.
law: The legal principle is that while fraud vitiates everything, it must be proven by the party alleging it.
The burden of proof (onus) to prove fraud lies on the person making the allegation, which in this case was the Insurance Company.
Merely alleging fraud is not the same as proving it in accordance with the law by adducing evidence.
application: The Court observed that the Insurance Company had not provided any evidence to support its claim of fraud.
The Court found that the Insurance Company had failed to discharge its onus (burden of proof) to prove the alleged fraud.
The Court accepted the lower court's finding that the premium was paid before the accident, which undermined the basis for the fraud claim.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the Insurance Company's argument, concluding that the company had failed to prove its allegation of fraud. Since the burden of proof was on the company and it did not provide the necessary evidence, its claim was dismissed, and it could not escape liability under the policy.

cases.case_name: Bhaurao Dagdu Paralkar v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: For its explanation of a legal concept (implied to be related to fraud).
For the observation that specifics of allegations such as fraud, undue influence, and coercion must be pleaded, as per Order 6 Rule 4 of the Civil Procedure Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A party alleging fraud, undue influence, or coercion must provide specific particulars in their pleadings and must establish these allegations with evidence.
obiter: Fraud is proved when it is shown that a false representation has been made knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly, careless whether it be true or false.
In cases of fraud, undue influence, and coercion, the parties pleading it must set forth full particulars, and the case can only be decided on the particulars as laid.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Even though fraud vitiates everything, merely alleging fraud does not amount to proving it. The Insurance Company, which has the burden of proof to establish its defenses, has not discharged its onus to prove the alleged fraud in obtaining the insurance policy.
legal_tests_applied: To avoid liability, an insurance company must not only establish the available defence(s) raised in the proceedings but must also establish a 'breach' on the part of the owner of the vehicle; the burden of proof for which is on them. (National Insurance Co. Ltd. v Swaran Singh)

Fraud arises from a deception committed by disclosure of incorrect facts knowingly and deliberately to invoke exercise of power and procure an order from an authority or tribunal. It must result in exercise of jurisdiction which otherwise would not have been exercised. (Shrisht Dhawan v. Shaw Bros.)
why_appellant_lost: The Insurance Company cannot be said to have established its defence, as it failed to discharge the burden of proof placed upon it.
The Insurance Company did not produce evidence, such as calling the Issuing Officer as a witness or using other means, to establish a factual position contrary to the respondent's claims.
The High Court and MACT made concurrent findings against the appellant based on the unrebutted evidence on record, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disbelieve those findings.
why_respondent_won: The evidence presented by the claimants, particularly the proposal form (Ex. R-5) and the insurance policy (Ex. R-6), went unrebutted by the Insurance Company.
policy_considerations: Insurance companies, with a view to avoid their liability, must not only establish the available defence(s) raised in the said proceedings but must also establish 'breach' on the part of the owner of the vehicle; the burden of proof wherefor would be on them.
